Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

The QRS complex of a paced beat or of a premature ventricular beat carries information about where
activation began. Regression and machine-learning models turn that information into a site on the
heart. A population model fitted on 1,012 pacing sites from 38
patients placed test sites with a mean error of about 11 to 12.5 mm on a generic left ventricle
[@zhou2018]; patient-specific models that learn from a few pacing sites during the procedure reached
about 6 mm in prospective case series [@zhou2021jaha]; and active methods choose where to pace next
[@missel2020; @meisenzahl2024]. This module derives why a QRS integral is a weighted sum of
activation times, fits localization by least squares, measures error along the heart surface, and
builds the Gaussian-process and expected-improvement loop behind active pace-mapping.

## From the field

- **Population, then patient.** In one group's work, a population regression on 120-ms QRS
  integrals gave mean test errors of 11.4 mm (support-vector regression) and 12.5 mm (linear
  regression) [@zhou2018]. With patient-specific coefficients learned from pacing during the
  procedure, the same group reported 7.2 ± 4.1 mm for 25 tachycardia exit sites after 3 remote and 5
  close pacing sites [@zhou2020], and 5.9 ± 2.6 mm for 26 sites in a prospective series of
  patients with structural heart disease using three leads (III, V2 and V6) [@zhou2021jaha].
- **A shell from CT instead of a full map.** Registering a CT-derived ventricular surface allowed
  the same approach without a complete electroanatomic map: 6.9 ± 5.7 mm for 20 tachycardias
  [@zhou2020ct]. In one patient, it was compared with ECG imaging from 120 body-surface leads: 8.9
  against 24.9 mm on 14 pacing sites [@zhou2018ecgi] (ECG imaging: m32).
- **Choosing the next pacing site.** A hybrid model trained on 38 patients and tested on a separate
  cohort of 8 localized left-ventricular pacing sites to 5.3 ± 2.6 mm using 5.4 ± 2.5 pacing sites
  [@missel2020]. A Bayesian-optimization method that models ECG similarity over the heart surface,
  and can avoid suggesting sites inside scar, reached 3.9 ± 3.6 mm with 8.0 ± 4.0 sites in
  simulation [@meisenzahl2024].
- **Training on simulations.** A classifier of outflow-tract origin (right or left) trained on 2,496
  simulated ECGs from 16 patient geometries reached accuracies of 0.86 and 0.84 on two clinical
  data sets, against 0.84 and 0.76 when trained on real ECGs alone; lead V2 carried the most
  information [@doste2022]. One of those test sets is an open database of 334 patients whose origin
  was set by the site of successful ablation [@zheng2020otva].
- **Small cohorts need intervals.** A logistic regression on ECG features, age and sex in 43
  patients separated right from left outflow-tract origin with a pooled ROC AUC of 0.910 (95% CI
  0.800 to 0.987) [@botis2026]. Reviews summarize the field and its open problems, such as external
  validation [@yang2024; @antoun2026].

## Derivations

Symbols: electrodes $e$, surface elements $j$ with activation times $\tau_j$, solid angle
$\Omega_{ej}$ of element $j$ seen from electrode $e$, potential scale $c$, integration window $T$,
feature vector $\mathbf x$ (one QRS integral per lead), origin coordinates $\mathbf r$, kernel length
scale $\ell$, signal scale $\sigma_f$, noise $\sigma_n$, posterior mean $\mu$ and standard deviation
$\sigma$.

### Why a QRS integral points to the origin

A simple model of ventricular activation puts a uniform double layer on the part of a closed
ventricular surface that has activated. In an infinite homogeneous medium, an electrode then sees a
potential proportional to the solid angle of the activated part (volume conduction: m02):
$\phi_e(t) = c \sum_j \Omega_{ej}\, H(t - \tau_j)$, with $H$ the unit step. Integrating over the first
$T$ milliseconds,

$$
x_e = \int_0^T \phi_e(t)\, dt = c \sum_j \Omega_{ej}\,(T - \tau_j)_+
= -c \sum_j \Omega_{ej}\, \tau_j \quad \text{when } T \ge \max_j \tau_j
$$ {#eq-m41-integral}

The last step uses $\sum_j \Omega_{ej} = 0$: from outside a closed surface, its solid angles cancel.
So a lead's QRS integral is a fixed, lead-specific weighted sum of activation times. The
activation times depend on the origin through distances along the heart, so the map from origin to
features is smooth but not linear. Zhou and colleagues used the 120-ms integral of each lead as
the feature [@zhou2018]; lab part A checks @eq-m41-integral against numerical integration.

**Key takeaways**

- A QRS integral weights activation times by how each lead sees each part of the heart.
- The map from origin to integrals is smooth, so nearby origins give similar features.
- The model ignores the torso boundary, wall thickness and repolarization; it is a tool for
  intuition.

### Fitting a localization model

Collect features $\mathbf x_i$ and known origins $\mathbf r_i$ (pacing sites) and fit
$\mathbf r \approx W^\top \mathbf x + \mathbf b$ by least squares. With $A = [X \;\; \mathbf 1]$,

$$
\begin{bmatrix} W \\ \mathbf b^\top \end{bmatrix} = (A^\top A)^{-1} A^\top R
$$ {#eq-m41-linear}

A **population** model is fitted once on many patients and maps features to a generic heart; a
**patient-specific** model is fitted during the procedure on that patient's own pacing sites. With $p$
features the fit needs at least $p + 1$ sites: 4 for three leads. Errors fall fastest when later
sites are close to the current estimate, because the map is close to linear over small regions
(lab part C) [@zhou2020].

### Measuring error on the heart

Localization error is a distance along the heart surface, not through the cavity. On a sphere of
radius $R$, for unit vectors $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$,

$$
d = R \arccos(\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v), \qquad \lvert \mathbf u - \mathbf v \rvert R = 2R\sin\frac{d}{2R} \le d
$$ {#eq-m41-geodesic}

so a straight-line error understates the distance along the wall, by more the farther apart the
points are. On a mesh, geodesic distance is computed as in m06; zhou2018 measured it on a generic
left-ventricular surface. The lab uses shortest paths along mesh edges, which are on average about 6%
longer than true geodesics on its mesh.

**Key takeaways**

- Least squares needs at least one more site than features.
- Population models generalize across patients; patient-specific models adapt to one.
- Report error along the surface, and say how it was computed.

### Choosing the next pacing site

Pace mapping compares the ECG of a paced beat with the target beat. A common score is the mean
correlation over the 12 leads:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{12} \sum_{l=1}^{12} \frac{\sum_t (a_l(t) - \bar a_l)(b_l(t) - \bar b_l)}{\sqrt{\sum_t (a_l(t) - \bar a_l)^2 \sum_t (b_l(t) - \bar b_l)^2}}
$$ {#eq-m41-corr}

It ignores amplitude and offset per lead. The score $f(\mathbf s)$ as a function of the pacing site
$\mathbf s$ is unknown but smooth. A **Gaussian process** with a squared-exponential kernel
$k(\mathbf s, \mathbf s') = \sigma_f^2 \exp(-\lvert\mathbf s - \mathbf s'\rvert^2/2\ell^2)$, conditioned on
the scores at the paced sites $S$, gives a posterior at any site [@frazier2018]:

$$
\mu(\mathbf s) = m + \mathbf k_*^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} (\mathbf f - m), \qquad
\sigma^2(\mathbf s) = \sigma_f^2 - \mathbf k_*^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} \mathbf k_*
$$ {#eq-m41-gp}

where $K$ holds the kernel between paced sites, $\mathbf k_*$ the kernel between $\mathbf s$ and
the paced sites, $\mathbf f$ the observed scores and $m$ a constant prior mean. **Expected
improvement** over the best score so far, $f^*$, has a closed form [@frazier2018]:

$$
\mathrm{EI}(\mathbf s) = \Delta\, \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{\sigma}\right) + \sigma\, \varphi\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{\sigma}\right),
\qquad \Delta = \mu(\mathbf s) - f^* - \xi
$$ {#eq-m41-ei}

with $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ the standard normal distribution and density and $\xi \ge 0$ a margin; when
$\sigma = 0$, $\mathrm{EI} = \max(\Delta, 0)$. It is large where the mean is high (exploitation) or
the uncertainty is high (exploration). Pacing where EI peaks, then updating, is the loop behind
methods such as @meisenzahl2024, which add constraints such as avoiding scar.

::: {.demo #m41-d1 badge="simulation"}

```{=html}
<div id="m41-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m41-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m41-d1-active-pacemap.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: a Gaussian process with a squared-exponential kernel (@eq-m41-gp; signal scale 0.5, noise
  0.01, length scale on the slider) and expected improvement (@eq-m41-ei) on a 31-by-31 grid of
  candidate sites 2 mm apart. The pacing sequence is recomputed exactly for each setting.
- The similarity landscape is illustrative: a main peak at the origin and a weaker peak elsewhere,
  standing in for a site whose paced QRS looks similar. It is not computed from an ECG model.
- Every sequence starts from the same two corner sites; the random rule uses a fixed seed.
- What would change the result: real similarity is noisy and depends on the leads and the window;
  sites inside scar cannot be paced; the surface is curved, not flat.
:::

::: {.demo #m41-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m41-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m41-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m41-d2-expected-improvement.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Exact: @eq-m41-gp with a squared-exponential kernel and noise 0.01, prior mean equal to the mean of
  the four scores, and @eq-m41-ei, evaluated on 241 points along the line.
- The four positions and scores are illustrative.
- What would change the result: hyperparameters are usually fitted to the data, not set by hand;
  with noisy scores the best observed value is itself uncertain [@frazier2018].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Pace-map correlation compares shapes, not amplitudes.
- A Gaussian process gives both an estimate and its uncertainty at every candidate site.
- Expected improvement trades a high estimate against high uncertainty in one closed formula.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where these tools sit.** Before an ablation for premature ventricular beats or ventricular
tachycardia, the 12-lead ECG is used to estimate the region of origin; during the procedure,
activation mapping and pace mapping refine it (m11, m24) [@zheng2020otva; @antoun2026]. The
methods in this module aim to make the estimate quantitative: a site on the patient's surface with
an error in millimetres.

**What the evidence is.** The results cited here come from retrospective and prospective case
series [@zhou2020; @zhou2020ct; @zhou2021jaha], a separate test cohort [@missel2020], simulation
[@meisenzahl2024], and retrospective classification with cross-validation [@doste2022; @botis2026].
Among them we found no randomized comparison of procedures with and without such a tool.
A review reports early data suggesting shorter procedures and less fluoroscopy [@antoun2026].

**What "ground truth" means.** In the open outflow-tract database, the origin is the site of
successful ablation, and only patients with a single source were included [@zheng2020otva]. In
pacing studies, the reference is the catheter position recorded by the mapping system. Both are
good references with limits: a lesion can succeed at a site near, not at, the origin, and excluding
multiple sources makes the task easier than the clinic.

In the terms of this module and m45:

- **Read the error metric.** A mean error in millimetres along the surface, with its spread, says
  more than "accurate".
- **Read the reference.** Pacing sites, ablation success and activation mapping give different
  ground truths.
- **Read the cohort.** Results on simulated hearts, on one centre's patients or on a separate cohort
  answer different questions.

## How experts think

Before trusting a model that places an origin from the ECG, ask:

1. **What was the reference?** Pacing coordinates, the site of successful ablation, or activation
   mapping [@zheng2020otva; @zhou2021jaha].
2. **What was split?** Pacing sites from one patient are correlated; a split by patient tests new
   patients (lab part B).
3. **How was error measured?** Along the surface or straight through, on a generic or the patient's
   own geometry (@eq-m41-geodesic).
4. **How many pacing sites did it need, and where were they?** Patient-specific and active methods
   trade pacing effort for accuracy (@eq-m41-linear; @eq-m41-ei).
5. **Simulation or patients?** Simulation-trained models need testing on real ECGs from other
   centres [@doste2022]; simulation results [@meisenzahl2024] are a target, not a clinical result.

One sentence to keep: **an origin estimate is only as good as its reference, its split and its
distance metric.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| QRS integral (@eq-m41-integral) | $x_e = c\sum_j \Omega_{ej}(T-\tau_j)_+$; $= -c\sum_j\Omega_{ej}\tau_j$ after full activation |
| Least squares (@eq-m41-linear) | $[W; \mathbf b^\top] = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top R$; needs $\ge p + 1$ sites |
| Surface error (@eq-m41-geodesic) | $d = R\arccos(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v) \ge$ chord $2R\sin(d/2R)$ |
| Pace-map similarity (@eq-m41-corr) | Mean Pearson correlation over 12 leads |
| GP posterior (@eq-m41-gp) | $\mu = m + \mathbf k_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2I)^{-1}(\mathbf f - m)$; $\sigma^2 = \sigma_f^2 - \mathbf k_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2I)^{-1}\mathbf k_*$ |
| Expected improvement (@eq-m41-ei) | $\Delta\Phi(\Delta/\sigma) + \sigma\varphi(\Delta/\sigma)$, $\Delta = \mu - f^* - \xi$ |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | What was done | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @zhou2018 | Population regression, generic left ventricle | 1,012 pacing sites, 38 patients, random 80/20 split |
| @zhou2021jaha | Patient-specific regression, three leads | Retrospective and prospective case series, 42 patients |
| @missel2020 | Hybrid population and active model | Separate test cohort of 8 patients |
| @meisenzahl2024 | Bayesian optimization of pacing sites | Simulation |
| @doste2022 | Classifier trained on simulated ECGs | Two clinical test sets, 365 patients |
| @botis2026 | Right vs left outflow tract, logistic regression | Retrospective, 43 patients, cross-validation |

**Rules of thumb**

- Split by patient; pacing sites from one heart are not independent.
- Pair a population model with patient-specific updates when pacing is possible.
- Quote errors along the surface, with spread, and the number of pacing sites used.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Why does the integral of the QRS carry information about the origin?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In a double-layer model, each lead's potential is the solid angle of the activated surface, so the
integral over the QRS is a lead-specific weighted sum of activation times (@eq-m41-integral).
Activation times depend on distance from the origin, so each origin produces its own pattern of
integrals across leads. The relation is smooth, which is why regression works, and nonlinear,
which is why patient-specific and local fits help.

</details>

**Q2. Population model or patient-specific model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A population model works before any pacing and needs no patient data, but it carries the spread
of anatomy and lead placement between patients: mean errors around 11 to 12.5 mm in @zhou2018. A
patient-specific model learns that patient's geometry and leads from a few pacing sites and has
reached about 6 mm [@zhou2021jaha], at the cost of pacing time. In practice the first gives a
starting region and the second refines it (lab part C).

</details>

**Q3. With three leads, what is the smallest number of pacing sites for a patient-specific linear
model, and why?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Four: three coefficients per coordinate plus an intercept (@eq-m41-linear). With exactly four the fit
passes through every site and has no redundancy against noise, so more are used in practice; the
cited system used at least five [@zhou2020ct].

</details>

**Q4. Why report error along the surface rather than straight-line distance?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Catheters and ablation act on the wall; two points on opposite walls can be close in straight
lines but far along the surface. The chord always understates the surface
distance (@eq-m41-geodesic), increasingly for distant points. State how the surface distance was computed
(mesh geodesic, edge paths) and on which geometry.

</details>

**Q5. A method localizes origins to 3.9 mm in simulation. How do you read that?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

As a target under ideal conditions [@meisenzahl2024]: the simulated ECGs come from the same model
family as the training, noise and lead placement are controlled, and the reference is known exactly.
Check the spread (± 3.6 mm there), the number of pacing sites (8.0 ± 4.0), the geometries and tissue
properties covered, and whether a clinical cohort was tested.

</details>

**Q6. What does the Gaussian-process length scale control in active pace-mapping?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

How far a measurement informs the estimate (@eq-m41-gp). A short length scale treats sites as nearly
independent, so the search explores widely; a long one smooths over the surface and can jump to a
wrong peak with confidence. Demo m41-d1 shows both. Hyperparameters are usually fitted, with care,
since few points are available.

</details>

**Q7. Explain expected improvement in one sentence, and say what happens where the model is
certain.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It is the average amount by which pacing at a site would beat the best score so far, given the
model's estimate and uncertainty (@eq-m41-ei). Where $\sigma = 0$ it reduces to $\max(\mu - f^*, 0)$,
which is zero at sites already paced: the rule never repeats a site without a reason.

</details>

**Q8. What can make a pace-map correlation misleading?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Correlation ignores amplitude and offset (@eq-m41-corr), so two different sites can give similar
shapes; the score depends on the leads, their positions and the time window; and noise or a changed
heart rate between the target and the paced beat alters it. Demo m41-d1 includes a second, weaker
peak to show how a search can be drawn to a similar-looking site.

</details>

**Q9. In lab part B, the random split by pacing site gives a lower error than the split by patient.
Why?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With a random split, sites from every patient are in training, so the model has seen each test
patient's geometry and lead positions. That estimates performance on new sites in known patients,
not on new patients. Note the design of each study: @zhou2018 split its 1,012 sites at random.

</details>

**Q10. A model trained on simulated ECGs is applied to patients. What can go wrong, and how was it
tested?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Simulations cover a limited range of anatomy, lead positions and tissue properties, so real ECGs may
fall outside it (lab part E). @doste2022 tested on two clinical data sets from other hospitals and
reported accuracies of 0.86 and 0.84, better than training on real ECGs alone; that is the right kind
of test, and it still covers only outflow-tract origins.

</details>

**Q11. A 43-patient model has a ROC AUC of 0.910 with a 95% CI of 0.800 to 0.987. What do you
conclude?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

That discrimination is probably good but imprecisely known: the interval is wide [@botis2026]. Adding
age and sex to ECG features changed the AUC by 0.057, not significantly (p = 0.104). It needs
external validation before it can be compared with established ECG criteria.

</details>

**Q12. How does learned localization differ from ECG imaging?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

ECG imaging (m32) solves an inverse problem with a torso and heart geometry and many body-surface
leads, and returns a whole map. Learned localization maps a few features from standard leads to one
site, using data from many patients or from pacing in this patient. In one patient, the pacing-based
regression was more accurate than ECG imaging for pacing sites [@zhou2018ecgi]; one case cannot rank
the methods in general.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds a double-layer forward model of a paced ventricle, fits population and
patient-specific localization models, runs an active pace-mapping loop with a Gaussian process, and
shows the cost of training hearts that differ from test hearts. It runs in about a minute.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Forward model and twelve leads; check @eq-m41-integral | synthetic |
| B | Population regression from twelve QRS integrals; split by patient or by site | synthetic |
| C | Patient-specific regression from three leads; random against sequential pacing | synthetic |
| D | Active pace-mapping: Gaussian process and expected improvement against random | synthetic |
| E | Training hearts that differ from test hearts | synthetic |
| F | Optional: a small neural network in PyTorch | synthetic |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m41_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m41_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m41_lab.ipynb).
- **Data:** synthetic only. We found no open data set with pacing-site coordinates that we could
  verify for automatic download. The open outflow-tract database [@zheng2020otva] labels origins as
  right or left outflow tract and sub-regions; it is a candidate for a later classification part.
- **Part F** runs only if PyTorch is installed.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A patient-specific linear model uses four leads. How many pacing sites does it need at
least?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Five: four coefficients plus an intercept (@eq-m41-linear).

</details>

**S2. On a sphere of radius 30 mm, two sites are 90° apart. Distance along the surface, and in a
straight line?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$30 \times \pi/2 = 47.1$ mm along the surface; $2 \times 30 \times \sin 45° = 42.4$ mm in a
straight line (@eq-m41-geodesic).

</details>

**S3. At a candidate site the posterior mean equals the best score so far and $\sigma = 0.2$. What is
the expected improvement ($\xi = 0$)?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.2\,\varphi(0) = 0.2/\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 0.080$ (@eq-m41-ei).

</details>

**S4. A paced ECG equals the target ECG with every lead doubled. What is the pace-map correlation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1: correlation ignores per-lead scale (@eq-m41-corr).

</details>

**S5. In @eq-m41-integral, why does the window length $T$ drop out once the whole surface has
activated?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Its coefficient is $c\sum_j\Omega_{ej}$, and the solid angles of a closed surface seen from outside
sum to zero.

</details>

**S6. True or false: a Gaussian process predicts the similarity score at an unpaced site with no
uncertainty.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. Away from paced sites the posterior variance grows towards $\sigma_f^2$ (@eq-m41-gp); that
uncertainty is what expected improvement uses.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Errors per patient.** Zhou and colleagues, Figure 1, the localization error for the pacing sites
  of each patient in the prospective series and the mean per patient [@zhou2021jaha;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8751877/)]. Compare the spread between
  patients with the mean (interview Q2).
- **Origins on a real surface.** The same paper, Figure 3, three premature-beat origins estimated on
  electroanatomic surfaces next to the clinically identified sites [@zhou2021jaha;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8751877/)]. This module: @eq-m41-geodesic.
- **From digital twins to a classifier.** Doste and colleagues, Figure 1, the pipeline from
  patient-specific heart models to simulated ECGs to a classifier tested on clinical ECGs, and
  Figure 2, simulated and clinical V2 and V3 QRS complexes side by side [@doste2022;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9412034/)]. Compare with lab part E.

## Further reading

- **Regression and patient-specific localization.** @zhou2018, @zhou2018ecgi, @zhou2020,
  @zhou2020ct, @zhou2021jaha.
- **Active and hybrid methods.** @missel2020, @meisenzahl2024; a tutorial on Bayesian optimization
  by @frazier2018.
- **Simulation-trained models and data.** @doste2022, @zheng2020otva.
- **Small cohorts and reviews.** @botis2026, @yang2024, @antoun2026.
- **AI competency areas.** Machine learning; Bayesian networks (Gaussian processes); search (shortest paths on the
  mesh); Markov decision processes (choosing the next pacing site). See the [AI competency
  map](../ai-competencies.qmd).
